niche.art.architecture.el-ladrillo-de-sa.title: El ladrillo de Salmona también dibuja espacio público
niche.art.architecture.el-ladrillo-de-sa.hook: Salmona trajo a Bogotá una arquitectura moderna de curvas, ladrillo visible y espacios abiertos.
niche.art.architecture.el-ladrillo-de-sa.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Corrected brick versus concrete construction and softened the anti-Corbusier story.

niche.art.architecture.el-ladrillo-de-sa.body: Rogelio Salmona trabajó casi diez años con Le Corbusier en París antes de volver a Bogotá en 1958. En las Torres del Parque, junto a la plaza de toros, trazó tres edificios curvos y recorridos abiertos que conectan la calle con los cerros. El ladrillo visible les da una textura reconocible, aunque su estructura también emplea hormigón: no se trata de ladrillo «puro». La Fundación Rogelio Salmona destaca ese diálogo entre materiales, geografía y espacios compartidos. Su obra no es una simple rebelión contra el maestro francés. Pregunta cómo puede un edificio moderno pertenecer a una ciudad concreta y, además, dejarle sitio al peatón.

recall.question: ¿Por qué el ladrillo de Salmona es una postura y no solo un gusto?
recall.answer: El ladrillo visible es parte de una respuesta al lugar, junto con las curvas y los recorridos públicos. Salmona también usó hormigón: la postura está en cómo combina materiales y espacios para relacionar el edificio con Bogotá.

niche.art.art-history.did-vermeer-cheat.title: Did Vermeer use a lens?
niche.art.art-history.did-vermeer-cheat.hook: Optical effects suggest a lens; technical studies also reveal ordinary perspective construction.
niche.art.art-history.did-vermeer-cheat.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Reframed optical hypothesis as contested; added gallery sources.

niche.art.art-history.did-vermeer-cheat.body: No surviving document says Vermeer owned a camera obscura. Yet some paintings show bright, soft-edged highlights that resemble optical effects, and Philip Steadman reconstructed room layouts consistent with a camera's viewpoint. In *Tim's Vermeer* (2013), Tim Jenison used a mirror comparator to make a striking imitation of *The Music Lesson*. That demonstrates a possible method, not Vermeer's actual one. Technical studies also find conventional perspective construction in his paintings. A lens might have helped him see, compose or transfer an image; none of those possibilities explains away his choices of colour, light and subject. The evidence remains an art-historical argument, not a solved trick.

recall.question: What does Tim Jenison's reconstruction actually establish about Vermeer?

options.text: That an untrained painter using an optical comparator can produce a Vermeer-like image
options.why: a proof of possibility, not of what Vermeer did.

options.text: That Vermeer definitely used a camera obscura
options.why: no document or device links him to one; the argument is inferred from the paintings.

options.text: That Vermeer had no unusual skill
options.why: critics reply that the interesting question was never the technique.

niche.art.art-history.the-exhibition-of-.title: The rejected paintings got their own exhibition
niche.art.art-history.the-exhibition-of-.hook: In 1863 rejected Salon paintings got their own show, and visitors saw what the jury had excluded.
niche.art.art-history.the-exhibition-of-.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Removed unsupported claim about Napoleon’s intent and instant vindication.

niche.art.art-history.the-exhibition-of-.body: In 1863 the Paris Salon jury turned away more than half the submitted works. Artists complained, and Napoleon III authorized a separate display where the public could judge the refusals. The *Salon des Refusés* opened in May. Visitors encountered paintings that later became landmarks, including Manet's *Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe* and Whistler's *Symphony in White, No. 1*. Contemporary reactions included mockery, not instant vindication. The event mattered because official rejection became the exhibition's organizing idea: the public could see what the gatekeepers had excluded. It did not end the Salon's authority overnight, but it gave artists another way to seek an audience.

recall.question: Why did the Salon des Refusés matter?
recall.answer: It displayed works rejected by the official Salon jury, giving artists and the public another place to see and judge them. Manet and Whistler were among the exhibitors; many visitors mocked the work at the time.

niche.art.color.the-dress.title: One photograph, three colours of dress
niche.art.color.the-dress.hook: The same pixels, on the same screen, split the internet in two — and the split was real, not a joke.
niche.art.color.the-dress.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Checked survey figures against the original study and tightened mechanism.

niche.art.color.the-dress.body: The dress was blue and black. Yet when its photograph spread online in 2015, many viewers saw white and gold, and some saw blue and brown. In a study of about 1,400 people, the three answers drew roughly 57%, 30% and 11%. Your eyes receive light reflected from cloth *and* illumination; your visual system estimates the lighting to infer the cloth's colour. This photograph leaves the lighting ambiguous, so different estimates can lead to different experiences even on the same screen. Neither group is pretending. The disagreement is a glimpse of the guesswork that ordinarily makes a white shirt look white under changing light.

recall.question: Why could two people see genuinely different colours in the same photograph?

options.text: Colour perception subtracts an estimated illuminant, and the photo was ambiguous about its lighting
options.why: so different assumptions yield different colours from identical pixels.

options.text: Their screens rendered the image differently
options.why: the effect persisted for people looking at the same screen together.

options.text: One group has better colour vision than the other
options.why: the study found a split in interpretation, not a deficiency in either group.

sources.title: Striking individual differences in color perception
sources.author: Rosa Lafer-Sousa, Katherine L. Hermann and Bevil R. Conway

niche.art.literature.el-paquete-que-nunc.title: El paquete de *Cien años de soledad* que quizá nunca se partió
niche.art.literature.el-paquete-que-nunc.hook: García Márquez dijo que envió su novela en dos paquetes; su editor recordó uno solo.
niche.art.literature.el-paquete-que-nunc.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Added opposing firsthand accounts; removed certainty about the postal legend.

niche.art.literature.el-paquete-que-nunc.body: García Márquez contó que el dinero no le alcanzó para enviar completo el manuscrito a Buenos Aires y tuvo que mandar una mitad primero. La escena es perfecta: una novela destinada a ser famosa viajando por entregas porque su autor estaba arruinado. Pero Paco Porrúa, el editor que lo recibió, le dijo al periodista Xavi Ayén que llegó entero en un solo paquete. Hay dos testimonios enfrentados y ninguna razón para convertir uno en certeza absoluta. Lo seguro es que Sudamericana publicó *Cien años de soledad* el 5 de junio de 1967. Incluso una historia sobre el viaje de un manuscrito puede convertirse en literatura.

recall.question: ¿Por qué sigue abierta la duda sobre el envío del manuscrito?
recall.answer: Porque García Márquez contó la versión de dos envíos, mientras Paco Porrúa le dijo a Xavi Ayén que recibió un solo paquete. Son testimonios contrapuestos; no conviene presentar ninguno como prueba definitiva del número de envíos.

sources.title: Xavi Ayén entrevista sobre Paco Porrúa

niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.title: Remember the point at infinity? Florence got there first.
niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.hook: Painters were drawing the point at infinity for two hundred years before a mathematician admitted it was a point.
niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.body:
In projective geometry you adjoin points at infinity so that parallel lines meet, and Euclidean geometry becomes a special case. It feels like a formal convenience invented to tidy up theorems.

It was invented by painters, and it was not a convenience — it was an observation. Sometime between 1415 and 1420 Filippo Brunelleschi ran a demonstration in Florence involving a painted panel of the Baptistery, a peephole drilled through it and a mirror, so a viewer could compare the painted building with the real one. By 1435 Leon Battista Alberti had written *De pictura*, setting out the construction: the parallel edges of a tiled floor converge to a single point on the horizon.

That point is not an artistic convention. It is where those parallel lines genuinely go. Girard Desargues (1591–1661), who knew the perspective literature, took it seriously and built the geometry — then was ignored so completely that his work survived through a handwritten copy Michel Chasles stumbled on in 1845.

Here is the correspondence, exactly.
niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.rigor:
Model the eye at the origin of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and the canvas as the plane $z=1$. A point $(x,y,z)$ with $z>0$ is painted at $(x/z,\,y/z)$ — which is precisely the map from $\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\}$ to homogeneous coordinates. A painting *is* a chart of $\mathbb{P}^{2}(\mathbb{R})$.

Take the ray through a scene point $p_0$ in direction $v$: $p(t)=p_0+tv$. Its image is

$$\frac{p_0+tv}{(p_0+tv)_z}\;\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\;\frac{v}{v_z},$$

independent of $p_0$. That limit is the vanishing point, and the computation says the two things a painter knows by instinct: it depends only on the *direction* $v$, so all lines parallel to $v$ share one vanishing point; and a direction with $v_z=0$ — parallel to the canvas — has no vanishing point at all, which is why the verticals of a building stay parallel in a painting.

The set of vanishing points of all directions lying in a given plane is a line on the canvas. For the ground plane, that line is the horizon. The horizon is the line at infinity, and you have been looking at it your whole life.

recall.question: In a perspective painting, why do a building's vertical edges stay parallel while the road's edges converge?

options.text: The verticals are parallel to the picture plane, so their direction has no vanishing point
options.why: only directions with a component towards the viewer converge.

options.text: Because artists choose to draw them that way for balance
options.why: the construction is forced by the projection, not chosen.

options.text: Because vertical lines are infinitely long and horizontal ones are not
options.why: length is irrelevant; only direction relative to the canvas matters.

niche.everyday.economics.the-popcorn-is-.title: Your popcorn purchase reveals a little about your ticket
niche.everyday.economics.the-popcorn-is-.hook: An optional bag of popcorn can reveal who is willing to spend more at the cinema.
niche.everyday.economics.the-popcorn-is-.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Added empirical paper and qualified metering inference.

niche.everyday.economics.the-popcorn-is-.body: Why is cinema popcorn so expensive? One economic answer is **metering**: charge everyone for entry, then charge extra to customers who choose concessions. Researchers using sales from Spanish cinemas found that buyers of high-priced snacks tended to have higher willingness to pay for admission, consistent with this kind of price discrimination. That does not prove every popcorn buyer loves the film more, or that all ticket prices would rise without snack sales. Costs, competition and studio contracts matter too. But it explains why a seller might prefer a modest entry price paired with an expensive optional extra: customers reveal some of their willingness to spend by choosing it.

recall.question: What does the cinema achieve by pricing popcorn far above cost?

options.text: It can collect more from customers who choose concessions
options.why: one study found that those buyers tended to value admission more.

options.text: It proves every popcorn buyer likes the film more
options.why: the evidence is an aggregate tendency, not a fact about each person.

options.text: It makes the admission ticket free
options.why: entry and concessions are separate charges, and tickets still have a price.

sources.title: Empirical Analysis of Metering Price Discrimination

niche.everyday.physics.the-curtain-that-.title: Your shower curtain can start its own vortex
niche.everyday.physics.the-curtain-that-.hook: A shower spray can set up a vortex that pulls the curtain inward; warm air may matter too.
niche.everyday.physics.the-curtain-that-.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Replaced “unsolved” headline with partial vortex explanation.

niche.everyday.physics.the-curtain-that-.body: Turn on the shower and a light curtain may lean inward. A common explanation invokes warm air rising; another points to moving air and pressure. In a fluid-dynamics simulation, David Schmidt found that the spray could set up a horizontal vortex with a low-pressure center that draws the curtain in. The work won a 2001 Ig Nobel Prize for a *partial* explanation. Which mechanism dominates can depend on the stall, spray and temperature, so the effect is a useful reminder that a familiar observation can have several interacting causes. Try cold water or a weighted hem and watch what changes.

recall.question: What did Schmidt’s shower-curtain simulation suggest?

options.text: The spray can create a low-pressure vortex that pulls the curtain inward
options.why: one mechanism among effects that can depend on the shower setup.

options.text: That static electricity must be the only cause
options.why: Schmidt modeled airflow and pressure, not static charge.

options.text: That warm water is required
options.why: the vortex account can operate without relying only on heat.

sources.title: List of Ig Nobel Prize winners

niche.everyday.physics.why-ice-is-slippe.title: Why a skate glides even when pressure cannot melt ice
niche.everyday.physics.why-ice-is-slippe.hook: Blade pressure alone cannot account for skating on ice kept well below freezing.
niche.everyday.physics.why-ice-is-slippe.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Corrected rink temperatures and avoided claiming one settled mechanism.

niche.everyday.physics.why-ice-is-slippe.body: A familiar account says the blade's pressure melts the ice beneath it. Pressure can lower ice's melting point, but too little to explain skating on much colder ice. Hockey surfaces are commonly kept several degrees below zero. A thin, mobile surface layer and heat generated as a moving blade rubs the ice are among the mechanisms researchers study. Their contributions change with temperature, speed and load; there is no single effortless explanation for every slippery surface. The useful correction is narrower than “pressure has no effect.” Pressure alone cannot make the water film that the old textbook story needs under ordinary skating conditions.

recall.question: What is wrong with the pressure-melting explanation of why ice is slippery?

options.text: Pressure alone cannot explain gliding on colder ice
options.why: surface effects and frictional heating also matter.

options.text: Skates are too wide to generate pressure
options.why: blade area is genuinely small; the problem is that even that pressure moves the melting point very little.

options.text: Only surface premelting matters
options.why: frictional heating can also contribute as the skate moves.

niche.everyday.statistics.berkeley-1973.title: The admission gap changed when the departments appeared
niche.everyday.statistics.berkeley-1973.hook: Berkeley’s 1973 aggregate admission gap changed meaning when researchers separated departments.
niche.everyday.statistics.berkeley-1973.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Corrected within-department claim and causal language; aligned diagram caption.

niche.everyday.statistics.berkeley-1973.body: Berkeley admitted about 44% of male applicants to graduate study in 1973, versus 35% of female applicants. The aggregate gap looked like evidence of discrimination. Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell checked decisions by department and found a different pattern: few departments showed significant sex differences, and the departures favored women about as often as men. Women had applied more often to departments with lower admission rates. Pooling those unequal mixes produced a misleading overall comparison. This is a lesson in selection and aggregation, not proof that no applicant faced bias. Before interpreting any group gap, ask which different populations were mixed to make it.
niche.everyday.statistics.berkeley-1973.rigor:
This is Simpson's paradox: an association can reverse under pooling. It is possible to have

$$\frac{a_i}{n_i}<\frac{b_i}{m_i}\quad\text{for every } i,\qquad\text{yet}\qquad \frac{\sum_i a_i}{\sum_i n_i}>\frac{\sum_i b_i}{\sum_i m_i},$$

because each pooled rate is a weighted average whose weights differ between the two groups.

The causal reading is the useful one. Department choice is associated with applicant sex and strongly predicts admission, so it can confound the aggregate comparison of admission by sex. The aggregate comparison conditions on nothing, so it mixes the within-department effects together with the difference in composition. Stratifying by department reveals the within-department comparisons, though it cannot by itself settle every causal question.

The trap is assuming stratification is always the fix. Condition on a variable sitting on the causal path *after* the treatment, a mediator, and you block part of the very effect you wanted to measure. Which way to slice the data is not a statistical question. It is a question about what caused what, and the numbers alone will not answer it.

recall.question: Berkeley's aggregate admission gap disappears once you condition on department. What made the aggregate misleading?

options.text: Department is a confounder, driving both where people applied and how likely admission was
options.why: and the sexes applied very differently.

options.text: The sample was too small to detect the real effect
options.why: nearly 13,000 applicants is ample; the problem is structure, not size.

options.text: Departments applied different standards to men and women
options.why: within departments the rates were close, and pooled they slightly favoured women.

options.text: Conditioning on more variables always removes bias
options.why: conditioning on a mediator can hide part of an effect or introduce bias.

sources.title: Sex Bias in Graduate Admissions: Data from Berkeley

niche.everyday.statistics.the-planes-tha.title: The bullet holes missing from the hangar
niche.everyday.statistics.the-planes-tha.hook: The data you can see is the data that survived long enough to be collected. Abraham Wald turned that sentence into a method.
niche.everyday.statistics.the-planes-tha.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Distinguished Wald’s documented method from the later slogan.

niche.everyday.statistics.the-planes-tha.body: In 1943 Abraham Wald studied damage on aircraft that returned from combat. The visible holes showed where surviving planes had been hit. They could not directly show where hits made a plane fail to return. Wald developed a method for estimating vulnerability from this selected sample, so armor could be placed where it would matter most. The neat slogan “armor the places without holes” captures the insight, but it is a later retelling, not a documented quotation from him. The general habit is sharper than the slogan: before trusting a dataset, ask what had to happen for an observation to enter it.

recall.question: What sampling problem did Wald's 1943 memoranda solve?
recall.answer: Returning aircraft are selected survivors, so their damage pattern under-represents potentially fatal hit locations. Wald used the selected data to estimate vulnerability and inform armor placement.

sources.title: A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors
sources.author: Abraham Wald

niche.food.coffee.caffeine-is-an-insecti.title: Your coffee is a plant's chemical weapon, badly aimed
niche.food.coffee.caffeine-is-an-insecti.hook: The coffee plant did not make caffeine for you. It made it to poison insects and sterilise the soil around itself.
niche.food.coffee.caffeine-is-an-insecti.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Softened the afternoon-crash mechanism from stated fact to the usual explanation.

niche.food.coffee.caffeine-is-an-insecti.body:
Caffeine is a defence molecule. It protects the coffee plant against herbivores, and it leaches into the soil where it suppresses the germination of competing seeds — the plant poisons its own neighbourhood to keep the space. Some plants also put small doses in their nectar, where it encourages the bees rather than repelling them.

We drink it. And here is the part that changes how you think about a cup: caffeine gives you nothing.

All day, your brain accumulates adenosine, a by-product that binds to receptors and produces the sensation of tiredness. Caffeine is shaped enough like adenosine to occupy those receptors without activating them. It does not add energy, or alertness, or capability. It sits in the doorway so the tiredness signal cannot get in.

The adenosine is still arriving the whole time. When the caffeine clears, all of it lands at once — which is the usual explanation for the afternoon crash.

recall.question: What does caffeine actually do in the brain?

options.text: It releases stored energy from glucose
options.why: caffeine supplies no energy and does not unlock any; the feeling of energy is the absence of a signal.

options.text: It blocks adenosine receptors without activating them, so the accumulating tiredness signal cannot be received
options.why: the adenosine keeps building up behind it.

options.text: It speeds up neuron firing directly
options.why: its primary action is receptor blockade, not direct excitation.

niche.food.coffee.juan-valdez-no-existe.title: El campesino más famoso del mundo nunca existió
niche.food.coffee.juan-valdez-no-existe.hook: Juan Valdez lo inventó una agencia de Nueva York en 1958. Fue la mejor política económica del café colombiano.
niche.food.coffee.juan-valdez-no-existe.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.food.coffee.juan-valdez-no-existe.body:
Un productor de materia prima no tiene precio propio: vende a lo que diga la bolsa de Nueva York. La Federación Nacional de Cafeteros, fundada el 27 de junio de 1927, entendió temprano la única salida posible: dejar de vender un commodity y empezar a vender una marca.

En 1958 la agencia Doyle Dane Bernbach inventó a Juan Valdez —sombrero, poncho, mula— con un objetivo estrecho y medible: que el consumidor estadounidense distinguiera el café 100% colombiano de las mezclas. Lo interpretaron tres actores en más de sesenta años, el más recordado Carlos Sánchez, entre 1969 y 2006. Ningún otro país cafetero logró nada parecido.

La prueba de para qué servía llegó el 4 de julio de 1989, cuando el Consejo Internacional del Café suspendió el sistema de cuotas de exportación que sostenía los precios desde 1962. El precio indicativo promedio pasó de 1,34 dólares por libra en el quinquenio anterior a 0,77 en el posterior: casi la mitad.

Cuando se cae el cartel, lo único que queda para defender el precio es que alguien prefiera tu grano por el nombre.

recall.question: ¿Por qué una marca como Juan Valdez es una decisión económica y no solo publicitaria?
recall.answer: Porque el productor de un commodity es tomador de precio: vende al precio internacional, sin margen propio. Diferenciar el producto —que el comprador pida café colombiano y no café— es la única forma de capturar un sobreprecio. Eso quedó a la vista en 1989, cuando se suspendieron las cuotas del pacto cafetero y el precio indicativo cayó de 1,34 a 0,77 dólares por libra.

sources.title: Federación Nacional de Cafeteros de Colombia

niche.food.cooking-science.la-arepa-no-e.title: La arepa de harina precocida siguió otro camino
niche.food.cooking-science.la-arepa-no-e.hook: La tortilla nixtamalizada y la arepa de harina precocida parten del maíz, pero lo procesan de maneras distintas.
niche.food.cooking-science.la-arepa-no-e.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Corrected niacin versus tryptophan and avoided treating all arepas alike.

niche.food.cooking-science.la-arepa-no-e.body: Una tortilla mexicana tradicional suele comenzar con maíz nixtamalizado: el grano se cuece en agua alcalina antes de molerlo. Ese tratamiento cambia la masa y puede mejorar la disponibilidad de la niacina, importante cuando el maíz domina la dieta. La arepa tiene muchas preparaciones; una versión actual muy común usa harina de maíz precocida, que no equivale a nixtamalizar. La Harina P.A.N. empezó a venderse en Venezuela en 1960 y convirtió una labor larga en mezclar, amasar y asar. La arepa es mucho más antigua que la bolsa. Confundir ambas historias borra lo que cambió con la industria y lo que ya sabía hacer la cocina indígena.

recall.question: ¿Qué distingue la nixtamalización del precocido de la harina de arepa?

options.text: Cocinar el grano en medio alcalino cambia la masa y puede aumentar la disponibilidad de niacina
options.why: no es simplemente cocerlo antes de moler.

options.text: Añade azúcar al maíz
options.why: el tratamiento es alcalino, no un endulzante.

options.text: Es idéntica a usar harina precocida
options.why: los dos procesos preparan el maíz de maneras diferentes.

niche.food.cooking-science.the-onion-is-.title: The onion makes its irritant only after you cut it
niche.food.cooking-science.the-onion-is-.hook: Cutting an onion lets two enzymes assemble the airborne compound that makes you tear up.
niche.food.cooking-science.the-onion-is-.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Tightened enzyme sequence and removed unsupported timing.

niche.food.cooking-science.the-onion-is-.body: An intact onion keeps key chemicals apart inside its cells. Your knife breaks those compartments. Alliinase enzymes produce sulfenic acids, and a separate enzyme identified in 2002 turns one into the volatile compound that reaches your eyes: syn-propanethial S-oxide. Tears respond to that irritant, not to an acid waiting in the whole bulb. The onion is a chemical machine triggered by damage. Chilling or cutting under water can reduce how much airborne irritant reaches you, though neither changes the reaction itself.

recall.question: Why does an onion only make you cry once it is cut?
recall.answer: Because the irritant does not exist in the intact bulb. Cutting ruptures cells, letting alliinase enzymes reach their substrates to make sulfenic acids; lachrymatory-factor synthase then converts one into the volatile syn-propanethial S-oxide. It is a defence assembled on damage.

sources.title: An onion enzyme that makes the eyes water
sources.author: Imai, Tsuge, Tomotake, Nagatome, Sawada, Nagata, Kumagai

niche.food.cooking-science.the-reaction-.title: The browning that needs sugar *and* protein
niche.food.cooking-science.the-reaction-.hook: Toasted bread and seared meat share a sugar-and-amino-acid reaction distinct from caramelization.
niche.food.cooking-science.the-reaction-.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Removed exaggerated scope and temperature threshold.

niche.food.cooking-science.the-reaction-.body: The smell of toasted bread or seared meat owes much to the Maillard reaction. A reducing sugar reacts with amino groups in food, setting off many further reactions that create aromas and brown compounds. Caramelization, by contrast, begins with sugars alone. Louis-Camille Maillard described the sugar–amino-acid chemistry in 1912; John Hodge later mapped major steps in its mechanism. This is why a cook often dries food before browning it: while water is evaporating, the surface struggles to get hot enough for the rapid reactions that build a crust. Crowding a pan slows that drying. Browning is chemistry, but it is also a problem of moisture and heat.

recall.question: What distinguishes the Maillard reaction from caramelisation?

options.text: Maillard needs an amino acid as well as a reducing sugar
options.why: caramelisation is the breakdown of sugars alone, which is why it tastes simpler.

options.text: Maillard happens only in meat, caramelisation only in sugar
options.why: Maillard browns bread, coffee, onions and almonds too.

options.text: Maillard requires water and caramelisation does not
options.why: surface water suppresses Maillard by holding the food near 100 °C.

sources.title: Dehydrated Foods: Chemistry of Browning Reactions in Model Systems
sources.author: John E. Hodge

niche.food.food-history.money-that-goes-.title: Cacao beans were small change you could eat
niche.food.food-history.money-that-goes-.hook: A tomato could cost one cacao bean in a 1545 price list. Even the beans could be counterfeited.
niche.food.food-history.money-that-goes-.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Removed disputed turkey price and simplified counterfeiting claim.

niche.food.food-history.money-that-goes-.body: In parts of Mesoamerica, cacao beans served as small change as well as an ingredient for drink. A 1545 price list from Tlaxcala gives the scale: a large tomato cost one bean; a small rabbit, dozens. The beans were countable and valued, but perishable. Fraud was possible too: accounts describe counterfeit beans filled or imitated with cheaper materials. Money need not be metal or paper. It needs people willing to accept it in trade, and enough trust that each bean is what it appears to be.

recall.question: What made cacao beans work as currency, and what made them fail?
recall.answer: Beans were portable, countable and valued in trade, so they could serve as small change. But they could spoil or be faked, making quality and trust a continuing problem.

niche.food.food-history.three-thousand-p.title: The Andes kept thousands of potatoes. Ireland had fewer bets.
niche.food.food-history.three-thousand-p.hook: The Andes kept thousands of potato varieties; dependence on the Lumper made Irish crops vulnerable in 1845.
niche.food.food-history.three-thousand-p.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Qualified variety count and added social causes of Irish famine.

niche.food.food-history.three-thousand-p.body: The Andean region still holds thousands of potato varieties, with different tolerances to cold and disease. In nineteenth-century Ireland, many poor households depended heavily on one productive variety, the Lumper. When *Phytophthora infestans* blight struck in 1845, that dependence magnified the loss. Genetic diversity alone would not explain the Great Famine: unequal landholding, poverty and political decisions shaped who starved and who could leave. But the crop contrast is a clear lesson in correlated risk. A field planted with similar potatoes may look efficient in a good year; when they share a weakness, one pathogen can threaten every household relying on it.

recall.question: Why is keeping thousands of potato varieties a rational strategy rather than inefficiency?
recall.answer: Varieties can differ in resistance to frost and pathogens, so a diverse crop spreads risk. Dependence on the Lumper increased Irish vulnerability to blight, although poverty and land policy also shaped the famine.

niche.games.chess-go.two-rules-and-no-en.title: A game you can teach in five minutes and lose at for fifty years
niche.games.chess-go.two-rules-and-no-en.hook: Go's rules fit on a postcard. The number of legal positions has 171 digits.
niche.games.chess-go.two-rules-and-no-en.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Go did not fall to brute force: AlphaGo won in 2016 with a neural network, not search. Corrected and trimmed to length.

niche.games.chess-go.two-rules-and-no-en.body:
Chess needs a page of rules: six pieces, each moving differently, plus castling, en passant and promotion. Go needs two. Stones are captured when they have no adjacent empty points left — no liberties. And you may not repeat a previous board position, which stops infinite loops. That is essentially it; the rest is turn order and how you count at the end.

From those two rules comes a 19-by-19 board with 361 points and roughly $2.1\times 10^{170}$ legal positions — more than the estimated number of atoms in the observable universe, by about ninety orders of magnitude. Every move offers hundreds of plausible options rather than chess's dozens, and games run far longer.

This is the interesting asymmetry: rule complexity and game complexity are almost unrelated. Tic-tac-toe has simple rules and a trivial game. Go has simpler rules than chess and a vastly larger game. What generates depth is not how much the rules say, but how much interaction they permit.

Which is why brute force beat Kasparov in 1997 and got nowhere here. Go fell in 2016, to a neural network that guessed at positions instead of counting them.

recall.question: What does Go's ko rule exist to prevent?

options.text: Endless repetition
options.why: it forbids recreating a previous board position, so capture-and-recapture cycles cannot loop forever.

options.text: Capturing large groups
options.why: group capture is exactly what the liberty rule is for and is entirely legal.

options.text: Playing on the edges of the board
options.why: edge points have fewer liberties but are perfectly legal to play.

niche.games.game-design.the-anti-landlor.title: The board game designed as propaganda against itself
niche.games.game-design.the-anti-landlor.hook: Monopoly was invented to teach you that landlords are the problem. It came with a second rule set nobody plays.
niche.games.game-design.the-anti-landlor.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Parker Brothers' token run of The Landlord's Game was 1939; sequencing corrected.

niche.games.game-design.the-anti-landlor.body:
In 1904 Elizabeth "Lizzie" Magie patented The Landlord's Game. She was a follower of Henry George, who argued that land rent enriches owners without their producing anything, and she built the board as an argument: go round, land on other people's property, pay, get poorer, watch one player end up with everything.

The design move that makes her a serious game designer is the second rule set. The same board could be played two ways. Under the monopolist rules you win by bankrupting everyone. Under the anti-monopolist rules, rents fed a common pot and every player got richer together. You played both, and the point was the comparison.

Parker Brothers bought Monopoly in the 1930s from Charles Darrow, who claimed to have invented it. In 1935 they bought Magie's patent too, for \$500, pushed her game aside within a year, and in 1939 printed a token run of it to secure the rights.

So the world's best-known board game is a teaching tool with its lesson removed — and the reason everyone finds Monopoly miserable and interminable is that it is *working exactly as designed*.

recall.question: What did Lizzie Magie's original 1904 game include that Monopoly does not?
recall.answer: A second, anti-monopolist rule set for the same board, in which rents went to a common pot and all players prospered together. Playing both versions was the point: the contrast was the argument for Henry George's land-value tax.

niche.games.probability-in-games.the-hou.title: A fair game can still ruin a small bankroll
niche.games.probability-in-games.the-hou.hook: In a fair game, your chance of bankrupting an opponent equals your share of the total bankroll.
niche.games.probability-in-games.the-hou.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Corrected finite-bankroll probability; certain ruin is a limit.

niche.games.probability-in-games.the-hou.body: Imagine a fair game in which you and an opponent exchange one unit on each round. Neither player has an edge. If you start with $i$ units and the total bankroll is $N$, your chance of taking it all before going broke is $i/N$. A richer opponent therefore has a better chance of outlasting you, even when every individual bet is fair. Against an *effectively unlimited* bankroll, continuing indefinitely means eventual ruin with probability one. That limiting case is often called gambler's ruin. The distinction matters: a merely richer but finite opponent can still lose. Fair odds on each flip are not equal odds for unequal fortunes.
niche.games.probability-in-games.the-hou.rigor:
Let your capital be $i$, the total in play $N$, and let you win each round with probability $p$, losing with $q=1-p$. Let $P_i$ be the probability you reach $N$ before $0$. Conditioning on one round,

$$P_i=pP_{i+1}+qP_{i-1},\qquad P_0=0,\; P_N=1 .$$

For $p\ne\tfrac12$ the solution is

$$P_i=\frac{1-(q/p)^{i}}{1-(q/p)^{N}},$$

and for $p=\tfrac12$ the walk is a martingale and $P_i=i/N$ — check the boundaries: $P_0=0$, $P_N=1$.

Now take the opponent to be much richer, so $N\to\infty$ with your stake $i$ fixed. In the fair case $P_i=i/N\to 0$: ruin with probability one. In the unfavourable case $q>p$ it goes to zero exponentially fast.

Notice what the fair case says. There is no drift against you, and you still lose everything — not because the walk trends down, but because only one of the two absorbing barriers is within reach.

recall.question: In a fair game with two finite bankrolls, what is your chance of winning everything?
recall.answer: If you hold $i$ of the total $N$ units, your chance is $i/N$. It approaches zero as the opponent’s bankroll grows without bound while yours stays fixed; with a finite opponent, it is never literally zero.

niche.games.puzzles.bridge-and-torch.title: Seventeen minutes before the bridge goes dark
niche.games.puzzles.bridge-and-torch.hook: The two slowest people should cross together. That sounds expensive until you count the returns.
niche.games.puzzles.bridge-and-torch.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.bridge-and-torch.body:
Four people need to cross a narrow bridge at night. They take 1, 2, 5, and 10 minutes to cross. At most two can be on the bridge; a pair moves at the slower person's pace. They have one torch, and whoever crosses must carry it. The torch lasts 17 minutes.

Sending the one-minute person back and forth sounds sensible. Try it: every return is cheap, but the slow people make separate trips. Can you get everyone across before the light goes out? List each crossing and add the minutes. The trick is to spend a return trip to save a much larger forward trip.

recall.question: What sequence gets all four across in 17 minutes?
recall.answer: The 1- and 2-minute people cross (2); 1 returns (1); 5 and 10 cross together (10); 2 returns (2); 1 and 2 cross (2). Total: 17.

niche.games.puzzles.cien-casilleros.title: Los diez casilleros que no se cierran
niche.games.puzzles.cien-casilleros.hook: Cien personas abren y cierran casilleros. Al final quedan abiertos exactamente diez.
niche.games.puzzles.cien-casilleros.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.cien-casilleros.body:
Hay cien casilleros cerrados, numerados del 1 al 100. La primera persona cambia el estado de todos. La segunda cambia cada segundo casillero; la tercera, cada tercero. Así hasta la persona cien, que solo toca el suyo. ¿Cuáles quedan abiertos?

Seguir a las personas una por una sería tedioso. Sigue, en cambio, al casillero 36: lo tocan exactamente las personas cuyos números dividen 36. Casi todos los divisores llegan por parejas, como 2 y 18. Pero uno puede quedarse sin pareja. ¿Cuál? Esa pequeña excepción explica por qué sobreviven abiertos tan pocos casilleros.

recall.question: ¿Qué casilleros quedan abiertos, y por qué?
recall.answer: Los cuadrados perfectos: 1, 4, 9, …, 100. Cada divisor provoca un cambio, y los divisores se emparejan salvo la raíz cuadrada de un cuadrado perfecto; por eso solo esos casilleros cambian un número impar de veces.

niche.games.puzzles.el-paseo-de-la-cabra.title: A la cabra le toca cruzar tres veces
niche.games.puzzles.el-paseo-de-la-cabra.hook: Para llevar a todos al otro lado, tendrás que traer a alguien de vuelta.
niche.games.puzzles.el-paseo-de-la-cabra.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.el-paseo-de-la-cabra.body:
Un campesino debe pasar un lobo, una cabra y un repollo al otro lado del río. La barca solo lleva al campesino y, como máximo, una cosa más. Si deja solos al lobo y la cabra, desaparece la cabra; si deja solos a la cabra y el repollo, desaparece el repollo.

¿En qué orden cruzan? El primer viaje parece obligado: la cabra. Después viene la parte incómoda. Llevar algo al destino no significa que deba quedarse allí. Dibuja dos orillas y anota quién queda en cada una tras cada viaje. La solución requiere retroceder con quien ya había avanzado.

recall.question: ¿Qué siete viajes resuelven el cruce sin dejar una pareja peligrosa sola?
recall.answer: Lleva la cabra; vuelve solo; lleva el lobo; trae de vuelta la cabra; lleva el repollo; vuelve solo; lleva la cabra. También sirve intercambiar lobo y repollo.

niche.games.puzzles.forty-three-quintill.title: Forty-three quintillion positions; twenty turns to solve
niche.games.puzzles.forty-three-quintill.hook: A Rubik’s Cube has 43 quintillion positions, but every one is within twenty face turns of solved.
niche.games.puzzles.forty-three-quintill.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Verified cube counts and twenty-move metric.

niche.games.puzzles.forty-three-quintill.body: A standard Rubik's Cube has 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 reachable arrangements. Corners and edges move, but parity and orientation constrain them. Despite that enormous state space, a computer-assisted proof completed in 2010 showed that every reachable position can be solved in at most **20 face turns**, counting a half-turn as one move. Some positions need all twenty, so the bound is exact. Counting quarter-turns only, the maximum is 26. The achievement was a bound on the *worst possible* scramble, not just a short solution to one puzzle.

recall.question: What does "God's number is 20" mean for a Rubik's cube?
recall.answer: That the cube's state graph has diameter 20 in the half-turn metric: no scramble, however evil, is more than twenty face turns from solved. Rokicki, Kociemba, Davidson and Dethridge proved it by computer in 2010; the quarter-turn answer, 26, followed in 2014.

niche.games.puzzles.four-queens-four-row.title: Sixteen squares, only two safe arrangements
niche.games.puzzles.four-queens-four-row.hook: Four queens fit on a four-by-four board, but one careless diagonal ruins everything.
niche.games.puzzles.four-queens-four-row.author: content-author

reviewed.notes: Rewrote title and opening; clarified the diagonal check.

niche.games.puzzles.four-queens-four-row.body:
Only two arrangements let four queens share a four-by-four board without attacking one another. A queen attacks along her row, column, and both diagonals. No other pieces block their lines of sight. Can you find one of the two?

One queen must occupy each row and each column, so you can record a candidate as four column numbers, one per row. That leaves only 24 arrangements to consider, but checking them blindly is no fun. Start with a queen in row one, column two. A diagonal now rules out more of row two than you might expect. See whether the remaining choices force the next two queens.

recall.question: Give the column of a queen in each row, top to bottom, with no attacks.
recall.answer: Columns 2, 4, 1, 3 work. They are all different, so no column attack; no pair's column distance equals its row distance, so no pair shares a diagonal. Reflecting the board gives 3, 1, 4, 2.

niche.games.puzzles.fourteen-fifteen.title: Swap 14 and 15; the prize becomes impossible
niche.games.puzzles.fourteen-fifteen.hook: Sam Loyd offered a prize for solving a puzzle that had been proved unsolvable eleven years earlier.
niche.games.puzzles.fourteen-fifteen.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Corrected parity proof scope and historical phrasing.

niche.games.puzzles.fourteen-fifteen.body: The sliding-tile puzzle swept America in 1880. Sam Loyd later offered a prize for solving a version with tiles 14 and 15 swapped. The money was safe: Johnson and Story had already analyzed the puzzle's parity. Each legal slide swaps the blank with one tile and also changes the blank's checkerboard colour. Those two changes preserve a combined even-or-odd signature. Swapping 14 and 15 without moving the blank changes only one part of it, putting the board in a different class from the solved state. You can slide forever and never cross that boundary. Here, “I cannot solve it” has a mathematical reason.
niche.games.puzzles.fourteen-fifteen.rigor:
Number the sixteen cells, treating the blank as tile 16, so a board is a permutation $\sigma\in S_{16}$. A legal move transposes the blank with a neighbour, which is a single transposition: it flips $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$. It also moves the blank one step, changing by one the taxicab distance $d$ from the blank to the lower-right corner.

So each move flips both parities, and the quantity

$$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\cdot(-1)^{d}$$

is invariant under every legal move.

The solved board has $\operatorname{sgn}=+1$ and $d=0$. Swapping 14 and 15 is one transposition and leaves the blank alone, so it has $\operatorname{sgn}=-1$, $d=0$ — the opposite value. No sequence of slides can connect them.

The invariant partitions all boards into two equally sized classes. The solvability theorem adds that every board in the solved state’s class can be reached; hence exactly half of the configurations are reachable.

recall.question: Why is exactly half of the 15-puzzle's positions unreachable, rather than some other fraction?

options.text: Each slide flips both the permutation's sign and the blank's taxicab parity, so their product is invariant
options.why: and that invariant splits the positions into two equal classes.

options.text: Because the board is 4 by 4 and even-sized boards are symmetric
options.why: board size is not what creates the invariant; the parity argument does.

options.text: Because the blank square must return to its corner
options.why: it must, but that alone does not rule out a swap of two tiles.

niche.games.puzzles.hanoi-keeps-doubling.title: The disk that doubles the whole puzzle
niche.games.puzzles.hanoi-keeps-doubling.hook: Adding one disk nearly doubles the work. What happens by disk 64?
niche.games.puzzles.hanoi-keeps-doubling.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.hanoi-keeps-doubling.body:
The Tower of Hanoi has three pegs and a stack of disks, smallest on top. Move the entire stack to another peg, one disk at a time, never placing a larger disk on a smaller one. One disk takes one move; two take three. How many moves for five disks?

To move the largest disk, every smaller disk must first move out of its way. Then you move the largest once, then move the smaller stack back on top. The entire smaller puzzle appears twice around one unavoidable move. Try building the count for three and four disks before answering five. Then picture doing the same with 64.

recall.question: What is the fewest moves for five disks, and what pattern gives it?
recall.answer: Thirty-one. If $M(n)$ is the minimum for $n$ disks, moving the bottom disk forces $M(n-1)$ moves before and after it: $M(n)=2M(n-1)+1=2^n-1$. For 64 disks, that is $2^{64}-1$ moves.

niche.games.puzzles.missing-corners.title: The chessboard that refuses thirty-one dominoes
niche.games.puzzles.missing-corners.hook: Sixty-two squares, thirty-one dominoes. The arithmetic fits; the tiling does not.
niche.games.puzzles.missing-corners.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.missing-corners.body:
Take an 8-by-8 chessboard and remove two diagonally opposite corner squares. You have 62 squares left. Each domino covers exactly two neighboring squares, so 31 dominoes seem perfect. Can you cover the board without gaps or overlaps?

Try a few placements and the obstruction stays hidden. Before moving a single tile, color the board the usual black and white. Every domino, whether vertical or horizontal, must cover one square of each color. What color are the two corners you removed? The answer is a tiny proof of impossibility, and it survives every clever arrangement you might try.

recall.question: Why can no 31 dominoes cover the board with opposite corners removed?
recall.answer: Opposite corners have the same color. Removing them leaves 30 squares of that color and 32 of the other. Every domino covers one of each, so 31 dominoes would require 31 of each color.

niche.games.puzzles.monty-knows.title: The host opens a door he knows is wrong
niche.games.puzzles.monty-knows.hook: One door disappears, but your first guess does not become any smarter.
niche.games.puzzles.monty-knows.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.monty-knows.body:
Three doors hide one prize and two goats. You choose a door. The host knows where the prize is, always opens a *different* door showing a goat, and always offers you the chance to switch to the only other closed door. Should you switch?

With two doors left, “half and half” feels natural. But the host did not open a door at random. He carefully removed a losing option while protecting your original choice. Ask a simpler question: how often was your first guess right? Switching wins precisely when that first guess was wrong. The host's knowledge is doing the work.

recall.question: Under the stated host rules, what is the chance of winning by switching?
recall.answer: Two-thirds. Your first choice is wrong with probability 2/3. Whenever it is wrong, the host must reveal the other goat, so switching takes you to the prize. Staying wins only when your first choice was right, probability 1/3.

niche.games.puzzles.nine-coins-two-weigh.title: Nine coins, one too light, only two weighings
niche.games.puzzles.nine-coins-two-weigh.hook: A balance scale has three answers, so two weighings can distinguish nine coins.
niche.games.puzzles.nine-coins-two-weigh.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.nine-coins-two-weigh.body:
Nine coins look identical. Exactly one is lighter than the rest, and you have a balance scale. Find the odd coin in at most two weighings. You may put any equal number of coins on each pan, and the scale can tip left, tip right, or balance.

Do not begin by weighing one coin against another. That spends a three-way observation on a tiny part of the problem. Instead, divide the nine coins into three groups of three. One weighing can identify the suspicious group. Then ask how a single weighing can identify one coin out of three. The scale's *balance* result matters as much as either tilt.

recall.question: How do two weighings locate the lighter coin among nine?
recall.answer: Weigh three coins against three. The lighter pan identifies the suspect trio; if the pans balance, the unweighed trio does. From that trio, weigh one coin against another. The lighter one is odd, or, if they balance, the third is odd.

niche.games.puzzles.nine-dots-no-box.title: Nine dots, four strokes, one invented boundary
niche.games.puzzles.nine-dots-no-box.hook: The puzzle never said your pen had to stay inside the square.
niche.games.puzzles.nine-dots-no-box.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.nine-dots-no-box.body:
Put nine dots on paper in a three-by-three square. Connect all nine with four straight, continuous line segments. You cannot lift your pen or retrace a segment. The lines may cross, and a segment may pass through more than two dots.

Most attempts turn at an outside dot, as if the square of dots were a wall. But the drawing has no border. Let your first line continue *past* the last dot. From there a diagonal can catch two dots that seemed impossible to reach together. The hard part is noticing a rule you supplied yourself and quietly removing it.

recall.question: What hidden assumption makes the four-line solution seem impossible?
recall.answer: That every turn must lie inside the square of dots. Start at the top-left dot, draw right through the top row and beyond; diagonal down-left through middle-right and bottom-middle to below bottom-left; straight up through the left column; then diagonal down-right through the center and bottom-right.

niche.games.puzzles.one-visit-three-swit.title: Three switches, one visit to the bulb
niche.games.puzzles.one-visit-three-swit.hook: A bulb can be off in two different ways: cold, or recently lit.
niche.games.puzzles.one-visit-three-swit.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.one-visit-three-swit.body:
Outside a closed room are three switches. Exactly one controls an incandescent bulb inside; the other two do nothing. The bulb starts off. You may flip switches as often as you like, but enter the room only once. When you enter, you must know which switch controls it.

Looking at the bulb gives only “on” or “off,” apparently too little for three choices. But an incandescent bulb retains heat after being switched off. You can arrange for one switch to leave the bulb lit, another to leave it dark but warm, and the third to leave it dark and cold. What sequence creates those three distinguishable outcomes?

recall.question: What do you do before entering, and what do the three observations mean?
recall.answer: Turn switch A on for several minutes, then off. Turn B on and enter promptly. Lit means B; dark but warm means A; dark and cold means C. This depends on a bulb that becomes warm while lit and stays warm briefly.

niche.games.puzzles.prisoners-follow-the.title: The boxes tell you which box to open next
niche.games.puzzles.prisoners-follow-the.hook: A team that looks doomed can win about 31% of the time by opening boxes in a strange order.
niche.games.puzzles.prisoners-follow-the.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.prisoners-follow-the.body:
One hundred numbered people face 100 numbered boxes. Each box hides one of their numbers, shuffled at random. Each person enters alone, may open at most 50 boxes, and must find their own number. Everyone wins only if *everyone* succeeds. They can agree on a strategy beforehand, but leave no messages.

Opening 50 random boxes each gives the team almost no chance. Yet one shared rule wins about 31% of the time. Your first box should bear your own number. Inside it is another number: what if that tells you which box to open next? Follow the chain and ask when it returns to you.

recall.question: What is the shared strategy, and when does it fail?
recall.answer: Each person opens the box with their own number, then the box named by the slip inside, and repeats. This follows a cycle of the hidden permutation. Everyone succeeds exactly when no cycle is longer than 50 boxes; under a random shuffle that happens about 31.18% of the time.

niche.games.puzzles.take-twenty-one.title: Twenty-one stones and a reply you can memorize
niche.games.puzzles.take-twenty-one.hook: In a pile of 21 stones, the first move can make every later move feel forced.
niche.games.puzzles.take-twenty-one.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.take-twenty-one.body:
There are 21 stones in a pile. Two people alternate removing one, two, or three stones. Whoever takes the last stone wins. You play first. Can you force a win against any reply?

Try starting near the end: with four stones and your turn, every choice leaves your opponent a winning final move. So four is a bad number to receive. Eight is bad for the same reason if you can always return the pile to four. Work backwards by fours until you reach 20. Your opening should hand your opponent that number; after each move, take just enough stones to complete a group of four.

recall.question: What first move forces a win from 21 stones?
recall.answer: Take one, leaving 20. If the opponent takes $k$ stones, take $4-k$. Together you remove four, leaving 16, then 12, 8, 4, and finally 0 after your move.

niche.games.puzzles.three-and-five-litre.title: Four litres with the wrong two jugs
niche.games.puzzles.three-and-five-litre.hook: A three-litre jug and a five-litre jug can measure exactly four. No marks needed.
niche.games.puzzles.three-and-five-litre.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.three-and-five-litre.body:
You have an unmarked three-litre jug, an unmarked five-litre jug, a tap, and a drain. You can fill a jug completely, empty it completely, or pour between jugs until one is full or the other empty. How do you leave exactly four litres in the five-litre jug?

No careful eyeballing is allowed. Each legal move lands on a state you can name: “two in the small jug, five in the big one,” for example. Try to get a *one-litre remainder* first. Once the small jug holds one, filling the big jug and pouring into the small one will leave four behind.

recall.question: What sequence leaves exactly four litres in the five-litre jug?
recall.answer: Fill the 5; pour into the 3, leaving 2 in the 5. Empty the 3; pour the remaining 2 into it. Fill the 5 again; pour from it into the 3 until that jug fills with one more litre. Four remain in the 5.

niche.games.puzzles.two-eggs-one-hundred.title: Two eggs against a hundred floors
niche.games.puzzles.two-eggs-one-hundred.hook: With two eggs, equally spaced test floors are a trap.
niche.games.puzzles.two-eggs-one-hundred.author: content-author

reviewed.notes: Clarified the monotone break-threshold premise.

niche.games.puzzles.two-eggs-one-hundred.body:
There is an unknown threshold: an egg survives a drop from any floor at or below it and breaks from every higher floor. You have two identical eggs and a hundred-floor building. A surviving egg can be reused. Find the highest safe floor, even if none is safe, while minimizing the *worst-case* number of drops.

If you test every tenth floor, the first egg may break late and the second must search many floors one by one. Instead, make the first jump large and each later jump one floor smaller. Why? After a break, your remaining one-by-one search should fit within the same total drop budget. What starting jump makes 100 floors reachable in fourteen drops?

recall.question: What is the minimum worst-case number of drops, and how does the first egg move?
recall.answer: Fourteen. Drop first from floor 14, then 27, 39, 50, and so on, shrinking each jump by one. If it breaks, test the unchecked floors below with the second egg. The reachable count is 14+13+⋯+1=105; thirteen drops cover only 91 floors.

niche.games.puzzles.two-ropes-forty-five.title: Two ropes, no clock, forty-five minutes
niche.games.puzzles.two-ropes-forty-five.hook: Uneven ropes are useless as rulers. They can still be clocks.
niche.games.puzzles.two-ropes-forty-five.author: content-author
niche.games.puzzles.two-ropes-forty-five.body:
Each of two ropes takes exactly one hour to burn from one end. Their thickness varies, so half a rope need not burn in half an hour. You have matches and need to measure 45 minutes. You may light either end of either rope, even while it is already burning.

A knot at the midpoint gives you no reliable time mark. Instead, ask what happens if fire eats a rope from *both* ends. Once you have a 30-minute event, you can make the second rope's remaining burn time shrink twice as fast. How would you arrange the lighting?

recall.question: How do the two ropes mark 45 minutes despite burning unevenly?
recall.answer: Light rope A at both ends and rope B at one end. A finishes after 30 minutes. Then light B's other end. B had 30 minutes of one-ended burn time left; from both ends it finishes in 15 more minutes.

niche.language.etymology.nobody-was-paid.title: The salt in your salary is a rumour
niche.language.etymology.nobody-was-paid.hook: Salary really does come from the Latin for salt. Roman soldiers really were not paid in salt.
niche.language.etymology.nobody-was-paid.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.language.etymology.nobody-was-paid.body:
Everyone has heard it: legionaries were paid in salt, hence *salarium*, hence "worth his salt". Half of that is true. The Latin *salarium* is genuinely built on *sal*, salt — that part is not in doubt.

The practice is. No ancient source records soldiers being paid in salt, or even given a salt allowance; the claim that they were is described in reference works as baseless. What the money had to do with salt, nobody actually knows.

A word can preserve a connection perfectly and lose the reason for it entirely.

recall.question: Which half of the "paid in salt" story survives scrutiny?
recall.answer: The etymology. *Salarium* is built on *sal* (salt) — but no ancient source attests soldiers being paid in salt, or receiving a salt ration. The link is real; the explanation is folk history.

niche.language.etymology.two-words-from-.title: One man in Baghdad named two-thirds of your maths vocabulary
niche.language.etymology.two-words-from-.hook: Algebra is named after a book about setting broken bones. Algorithm is named after the man who wrote it.
niche.language.etymology.two-words-from-.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Softened an unverifiable superlative about the word 'algorithm'.

niche.language.etymology.two-words-from-.body:
Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī, working in Baghdad sometime between 813 and 833, wrote a book with *al-jabr* in the title. The word did not mean anything mathematical yet: *al-jabr* was what a surgeon did to a broken bone — forcing the parts back together. Al-Khwārizmī borrowed it for what you do to an equation when you move a term across the equals sign and make the pieces whole again.

Latin translators turned *al-jabr* into *algebra* and kept it.

Then they did it again with his name. Al-Khwārizmī also wrote the manual that taught Europe to calculate with Hindu–Arabic numerals instead of Roman ones, and the Latin versions open with *Algoritmi* — his name, mangled. The step-by-step method in the book took on the name of the man: *algorism*, eventually *algorithm*.

So every time you say "algorithm" you are mispronouncing a place name — al-Khwārizmī means "the man from Khwarazm", a region south of the Aral Sea. Twelve centuries later it is one of the most-used words in technology.

recall.question: Where do the words "algebra" and "algorithm" come from, and what did *al-jabr* originally mean?
recall.answer: Both trace to one 9th-century scholar. *Algebra* comes from *al-jabr* in the title of his book — a word that originally meant bone-setting, the forcing back together of broken parts. *Algorithm* comes from the Latinisation of his own name, *Algoritmi*.

niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.title: The one word almost every language agrees on
niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.hook: Ten unrelated languages, five continents, one nearly identical syllable for "I did not catch that".
niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.body:
Words are supposed to be arbitrary. *Dog*, *perro*, *inu* — no reason for any of them, which is why unrelated languages sound nothing alike. Then there is *huh?*

Mark Dingemanse, Francisco Torreira and N. J. Enfield recorded ordinary conversation in ten languages from five continents — Siwu in Ghana, Cha'palaa in Ecuador, Murriny Patha in Australia, Icelandic, Mandarin, Spanish — and found the same item in each: a short, questioning syllable, low front vowel, no consonants to speak of, rising intonation. Close enough that the similarity is far beyond chance.

Their explanation is not shared ancestry, and not instinct. It is convergent evolution. Every conversation on Earth faces the same engineering problem: you missed something, and you have a fraction of a second to say so before the speaker moves on. The solution has to be minimal — one syllable, producible with a half-open mouth, unmistakably a question. Selection pressure that specific yields the same shape everywhere.

And the second claim of the paper is the subtler one.
niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.rigor:
The authors argue *huh?* is a **word**, not a grunt, and the distinction is testable. A cry of pain or a sneeze is involuntary and its form is not language-specific. A word is conventional, learned, and fitted to the sound system of its language.

Their evidence: the vowel in *huh?* is not identical across languages but varies *within each language's own vowel inventory*, and the intonation follows the language's own question prosody — rising in English and Spanish, falling in Icelandic, where questions fall. A reflex would not be locally adapted like that. Children have to learn it.

So the argument is a two-sided one, and both sides matter: the *function* is universal because the interactional problem is universal, while the *form* is conventional because it has been fitted to each language. The similarity is not inheritance from a common ancestor but the same problem solved the same way, independently, thousands of times — the linguistic version of the eye evolving again and again.

recall.question: What is the evidence that *huh?* is a learned word rather than an involuntary noise?

options.text: It appears in every recorded language
options.why: universality is compatible with a reflex; sneezes are universal too.

options.text: Its vowel and intonation are fitted to each language's own sound system and question prosody
options.why: a reflex would not vary language by language in exactly that way.

options.text: It is written down in dictionaries
options.why: orthography reflects convention about spelling, not whether the item is linguistic.

sources.title: Is "Huh?" a Universal Word? Conversational Infrastructure and the Convergent Evolution of Linguistic Items
sources.author: Dingemanse, Torreira and Enfield

niche.language.spanish.el-abecedario-per.title: En 2010 el español perdió dos letras
niche.language.spanish.el-abecedario-per.hook: La RAE prometió en 1713 limpiar y fijar el idioma. Trescientos años después su mejor trabajo ha sido ceder.
niche.language.spanish.el-abecedario-per.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: 'Siglo y medio' was wrong: ch and ll were letters from the 1754 Ortografia until 2010.

niche.language.spanish.el-abecedario-per.body:
La *ch* y la *ll* fueron letras del abecedario desde la *Ortografía* de 1754. Ya no lo son. La *Ortografía de la lengua española* de 2010 las degradó a dígrafos: dos letras escritas juntas, como la *rr*. El abecedario quedó en veintisiete.

No fue un capricho. En 1994 las academias ya habían decidido ordenarlas dentro de la *c* y la *l* para alfabetizar como el resto del mundo latino, y en 2010 sacaron la conclusión: si no se ordenan aparte, no son letras aparte. Lo que no cambió fue la escritura. *Chocolate* sigue escribiéndose igual.

Lo interesante es quién decide. La Academia nació el 6 de julio de 1713, por iniciativa del marqués de Villena, con un lema de crisol y fuego: *limpia, fija y da esplendor*. Pero desde hace décadas no manda sola: la RAE y las otras veintitrés academias forman la ASALE, y las normas se pactan entre todas. Bogotá, Ciudad de México y Buenos Aires votan.

Una institución fundada para purificar terminó haciendo estadística descriptiva del uso.

recall.question: ¿Qué cambió exactamente en 2010 con la ch y la ll?

options.text: Dejaron de considerarse letras del abecedario y pasaron a ser dígrafos
options.why: la escritura no cambió; lo que cambió fue el inventario de letras.

options.text: Desaparecieron de la escritura del español
options.why: sigue escribiéndose *chocolate* y *llave* exactamente igual.

options.text: Empezaron a ordenarse dentro de la c y la l
options.why: eso ya se había decidido en 1994; 2010 sacó la conclusión.

niche.language.spanish.la-enie-casi-se-p.title: La letra que inventó la pereza y que Bruselas casi borra
niche.language.spanish.la-enie-casi-se-p.hook: La ñ nació como una trampa de copistas con prisa. En 1991 Bruselas estuvo a punto de borrarla por libre comercio.
niche.language.spanish.la-enie-casi-se-p.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Title reworded for grammar; the 1991 EEC keyboard dispute and the decree of 23 April 1993 check out.

niche.language.spanish.la-enie-casi-se-p.body:
La ñ empezó siendo un atajo. En los monasterios medievales el pergamino era caro y la mano se cansaba, así que la doble *nn* del latín —*annus*, *pannus*— se abreviaba escribiendo una sola *n* con una rayita encima. Esa rayita, la tilde, es literalmente una *n* aplastada.

El atajo se volvió sonido, y el sonido se volvió letra. Hoy la ñ no es solo española: la usan el gallego, el asturiano, el euskera, el aimara, el quechua y el guaraní. El inglés se la lleva prestada cada vez que escribe *jalapeño* o *El Niño*.

En 1991 casi desaparece de los teclados. Algunos fabricantes, con el respaldo de la Comunidad Económica Europea, argumentaron que obligar a incluir la ñ en los teclados vendidos en España era proteccionismo disfrazado y violaba la libre circulación de mercancías. España respondió el 23 de abril de 1993 con un real decreto que mantuvo la obligación.

Una raya que ahorraba tinta en el siglo XII terminó defendida como patrimonio cultural en un tribunal de comercio.

recall.question: ¿De dónde sale la tilde de la ñ?
recall.answer: De una abreviatura. Los copistas medievales escribían la doble *nn* latina como una sola *n* con una rayita encima para ahorrar espacio y esfuerzo; esa rayita es una *n* comprimida. Después el dígrafo abreviado se consolidó como letra propia.

niche.language.spanish.tres-maneras-de-d.title: Un país, tres segundas personas
niche.language.spanish.tres-maneras-de-d.hook: En Medellín te dicen vos, en Bogotá usted y en Cartagena tú. Los tres son restos de la misma pelea del siglo XVI.
niche.language.spanish.tres-maneras-de-d.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Fixed a tu/vos mix inside one clause ('uses ... venis').

niche.language.spanish.tres-maneras-de-d.body:
Colombia hace algo que casi ningún idioma tolera: usa tres pronombres distintos para hablarle a una sola persona, y el que uses delata de dónde vienes. Paisas, caldenses y caleños vosean. El altiplano bogotano ustedea incluso con los amigos y con el perro. La costa Caribe tutea.

El origen está en una inflación de cortesía. El latín *vos* era plural y servía para tratar con respeto a una sola persona; de tanto usarse, se gastó. España resolvió el desgaste con *vuestra merced* —que se comprimió hasta *usted*— y abandonó el *vos*. América no se enteró toda al tiempo: las regiones con tráfico constante hacia la metrópoli adoptaron el cambio; las lejanas conservaron el *vos* del siglo XVI.

Por eso el voseo no es una deformación: es la forma antigua, conservada en los lugares a los que la moda no llegó. Antioquia y el Valle hablan, en este punto, más parecido al español de Cervantes que Madrid.

Y la conjugación se conservó con él: *vos sos*, *vos tenés*, *vos cantás*, *vení*, *comé* — imperativos a los que solo se les cayó la *d* final de *venid* y *comed*.

recall.question: ¿Por qué el voseo aparece justo en las regiones más alejadas de los grandes centros coloniales?
recall.answer: Porque el voseo es la forma vieja, no una innovación. España sustituyó el *vos* por *tú* y *vuestra merced* (de donde sale *usted*), y el cambio viajó con el contacto: las zonas con tráfico constante hacia la metrópoli lo adoptaron, y las aisladas conservaron el *vos* del siglo XVI.

niche.language.untranslatable.the-word-e.title: There is no English word for the best part of lunch
niche.language.untranslatable.the-word-e.hook: English can describe sitting at the table long after the plates are cleared. It just needs a whole sentence to do it.
niche.language.untranslatable.the-word-e.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Hook's 'eleven words' did not count out; replaced.

niche.language.untranslatable.the-word-e.body:
*Sobremesa*: the stretch of time that starts when dessert is served and ends whenever the conversation does. Nobody stands up. Coffee appears, maybe an aguardiente. The meal is over and the table is not.

"Untranslatable" is an overstatement — that paragraph just translated it. What English lacks is a *single word*, a different and more interesting claim: languages hand short labels to whatever their speakers do often enough to need one.

The gap is not about concepts. It is about how long you sit there.

recall.question: What does a so-called "untranslatable" word usually mean?
recall.answer: Not that the idea cannot be expressed — almost anything can be paraphrased — but that the other language has no *single word* for it. Short labels get minted for what a culture does often, so lexical gaps map habits rather than thoughts.

niche.language.writing-systems.hangul-is.title: The alphabet that draws the inside of your mouth
niche.language.writing-systems.hangul-is.hook: Korean consonants are not arbitrary squiggles. Each one is a small drawing of what your tongue is doing.
niche.language.writing-systems.hangul-is.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.language.writing-systems.hangul-is.body:
Latin letters are the descendants of pictures of things — A was an ox head, once, upside down. They tell you nothing about the sound. Hangul does something no other major script does: the letter *is* a diagram of the organ making the noise.

Announced around 1443 and published in 1446 under Sejong the Great, its five basic consonants each depict an articulation. ㄱ shows the back of the tongue blocking the soft palate, which is exactly what you do to say *k*. ㅁ is a mouth, and it is *m*. ㄴ is the tongue tip touching behind the teeth, *n*. Then the system compounds: add a stroke for more breath, so ㄷ becomes ㅌ, plain *t* becoming aspirated *t*.

The companion volume, the *Hunminjeongeum Haerye*, explains all of this in writing — which makes Hangul one of the very few scripts in history whose designers left behind their reasoning.

Sejong's stated motive was blunt: Korean sounds do not fit Chinese characters, and ordinary people could not learn them. It was engineering aimed at literacy, and it worked.

recall.question: What makes Hangul's consonant letters unusual among the world's scripts?

options.text: They were derived from simplified Chinese characters
options.why: the *Haerye* explicitly grounds them in articulation instead.

options.text: Their shapes depict the position of the speech organs that produce them
options.why: ㅁ is a mouth, ㄱ is the tongue blocking the palate.

options.text: Each letter stands for a whole syllable
options.why: syllables are built by stacking letters into blocks, but the letters themselves are phonemes.

niche.language.writing-systems.the-man-w.title: A man who could not read invented a writing system
niche.language.writing-systems.the-man-w.hook: Sequoyah could not read a word of any language. He worked out what writing was from first principles, and then built one.
niche.language.writing-systems.the-man-w.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.language.writing-systems.the-man-w.body:
Every other script on Earth was adapted from an older script, or built by people who already knew how writing worked. The Cherokee syllabary is the exception that historians keep coming back to: Sequoyah was illiterate in every language, including his own, when he started.

He had seen white settlers reading — "talking leaves" — and reasoned from the outside that marks could hold speech. Through the late 1810s he tried a symbol per word, which failed under its own weight, then switched to a symbol per syllable. Cherokee has few enough syllables for that to work. He ended with 86 characters, later trimmed to 85 for the printing press.

The adoption is the astonishing part. By 1825 the majority of Cherokee could read and write in it, a language that had been unwritten a decade earlier. On 21 February 1828 the *Cherokee Phoenix* began publishing at New Echota in Cherokee and English, the first newspaper in a Native American language.

One man, working alone, compressed several thousand years of writing's development into about a decade.

recall.question: Why was a syllabary — rather than an alphabet — the right design for Cherokee?
recall.answer: Sequoyah first tried one symbol per word and drowned in symbols. Cherokee has a small enough inventory of syllables that one symbol per syllable is manageable: 86 characters covered the language, and learners could start reading almost immediately without analysing sounds below the syllable.

niche.music.latam.la-cumbia-tiene-tres-p.title: La cumbia no tiene una sola genealogía
niche.music.latam.la-cumbia-tiene-tres-p.hook: En la cumbia se oyen encuentros entre tradiciones indígenas, africanas y europeas, sin fronteras limpias entre ellas.
niche.music.latam.la-cumbia-tiene-tres-p.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Removed tidy one-culture-per-instrument genealogy.

niche.music.latam.la-cumbia-tiene-tres-p.body: En la cumbia del Caribe colombiano se cruzan prácticas indígenas, africanas y europeas. Se oyen gaitas o caña de millo, maracas y tambores; el canto y el baile también guardan historias de encuentro y transformación. Es tentador asignar cada sonido a un «padre» único: una flauta indígena, un tambor africano, una copla española. Esa fórmula ayuda a escuchar capas, pero simplifica siglos de intercambio entre músicos que cambiaron instrumentos y ritmos al tocarlos juntos. En el siglo XX, orquestas como la de Lucho Bermúdez llevaron esas formas a nuevos públicos. La cumbia siguió viajando y tomando acentos propios en otros países latinoamericanos.

recall.question: ¿Por qué «tres padres» simplifica la historia de la cumbia?

options.text: Porque los músicos transformaron instrumentos y formas al tocarlos juntos
options.why: no se puede asignar cada rasgo a una sola fuente intacta.

options.text: Porque la cumbia nació sin encuentros culturales
options.why: precisamente se formó en una historia de contactos.

options.text: Porque solo importan las orquestas del siglo XX
options.why: las orquestas ampliaron su público, pero había prácticas anteriores.

niche.music.recording.the-voice-that-wai.title: The voice recorded in 1860 and heard in 2008
niche.music.recording.the-voice-that-wai.hook: The first recording of a human voice was made in 1860 by a man who had no intention of ever playing it back.
niche.music.recording.the-voice-that-wai.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Checked date and playback against Library of Congress account.

niche.music.recording.the-voice-that-wai.body: Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville's phonautograph drew sound waves as lines on soot-darkened paper. It had no way to play them back. On 9 April 1860, someone sang *Au clair de la lune* into his machine, leaving a trace that spent generations silent in an archive. In 2008 researchers scanned that trace and converted the image into sound. The Library of Congress recognizes these phonautograms as early recordings of the human voice, made before Edison's playback-capable phonograph. Scott had built a way to *see* sound; digital tools supplied the missing way to hear it. The paper outlived the machine's original purpose.

recall.question: Why could Scott's 1860 phonautogram be heard in 2008 but not in 1860?
recall.answer: The phonautograph traced sound as a visual line on soot-blackened paper and had no playback mechanism at all — Scott wanted sound to be read, not heard. In 2008 the IRENE system at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory scanned those tracings as images and converted them into sound digitally.
